items.s: A nurse is calculating a 1-minute Apgar score for a newborn whose body is pink but whose hands and feet remain blue. How many points should be assigned for the color component?
items.r: In the Apgar appearance/color component, a pink body with blue extremities (acrocyanosis) receives 1 point. Generalized pallor or cyanosis receives 0 points, and completely pink color receives 2 points.

src.l: Table/section describing Appearance (color): blue/pale = 0; pink body with blue extremities = 1; completely pink = 2.

o.A: Clean the stump routinely with rubbing alcohol after diaper changes and keep it covered with dry gauze until separation.
o.B: Keep it clean and dry, fold the diaper below it, and use sponge baths until it falls off.
o.C: Apply petroleum jelly routinely so the stump remains moist until separation.
o.D: Begin routine tub baths while the stump is attached as long as it is dried afterward.

o.A: Avoid local comfort measures until the swelling resolves spontaneously.
o.B: Use a warm sitz bath as the preferred first intervention immediately after birth.
o.C: Apply an ice pack for short periods to reduce swelling and pain.
o.D: Apply continuous dry heat to the perineum during the first 24 hours.

items.s: A client is 8 hours postpartum after a vaginal birth and reports perineal swelling and soreness. Which comfort measure is appropriate during the first 24 hours?
items.r: MedlinePlus postpartum instructions recommend ice packs during the first 24 hours after vaginal birth to reduce perineal swelling and pain. Warm baths are generally introduced after the first 24 hours.

src.n: NIH/NLM MedlinePlus — After vaginal delivery: in the hospital
src.l: Perineal-care section: ice packs during the first 24 hours; warm baths after 24 hours.
src.v: MedlinePlus patient instruction review date 2024-11-08; rechecked 2026-08-15.

o.A: Keep the client supine and elevate the legs to increase venous return without changing trunk position.
o.B: Turn the client onto a side to relieve gravid-uterus compression of major vessels and restore venous return.
o.C: Give a carbohydrate drink before repositioning because late-pregnancy supine dizziness usually reflects hypoglycemia.
o.D: Continue the ultrasound with the client flat for several minutes and reposition if the dizziness fails to resolve spontaneously.

o.A: Begin with the face and upper body, proceed downward, and perform perineal care last.
o.B: Perform perineal care first because the most contaminated area should be completed before cleaner regions.
o.C: Wash the feet and legs first, then the upper body, and perform perineal care midway through the bath.
o.D: Choose the sequence according to convenience as long as the washcloth is rinsed between body regions.

o.A: Screen when the client reports persistent sadness, loss of interest, or another symptom suggesting a postpartum mood disorder.
o.B: Omit postpartum screening if depression screening was already completed during pregnancy.
o.C: Refer all mood screening to a mental-health specialist rather than using validated tools in obstetric care.
o.D: Screen for depression and anxiety with a validated instrument and have systems for timely assessment and follow-up.

o.A: The baby’s mouth is open wide over the areola, the lips are turned outward, and the chin rests against the breast.
o.B: The baby’s lips are tucked inward and the chin remains away from the breast.
o.C: The baby attaches mainly to the nipple tip and repeatedly clicks during sucking.
o.D: The parent has persistent sharp nipple pain and the baby’s cheeks pull inward with each suck.

o.A: Use annual cervical cytology after sexual activity begins because frequent testing is the safest approach for average-risk adults.
o.B: Stop screening after one normal adult test when there is no history of cervical disease or immunocompromise.
o.C: Base screening on age, test strategy, prior screening history, and risk factors, with individualized follow-up when risk is higher.
o.D: Select the interval mainly from patient preference because current recommendations do not distinguish among age groups and test strategies.

o.A: Limit contact with the infant because seeing or holding the baby generally intensifies bereavement and should be avoided.
o.B: Use a standard contact and memorial routine for families after stillbirth so staff can provide consistent bereavement care.
o.C: Delay discussion of remembrance or cultural practices until discharge so the family can first process the loss.
o.D: Offer the opportunity to hold the infant and follow desired cultural or religious practices while providing individualized support.
